```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

This vignette covers what to do with a fitted model: which standard errors to
use, how to predict and simulate, which residuals and diagnostics are
available, and how to compare models, including when a likelihood-ratio
(LR) test is valid and when it is not.

```{r setup}
library(flexCountReg)
data("washington_roads")
d <- washington_roads
```

## Standard errors

Every estimator has a `stderr` argument with three choices. The choice is
made when the model is fit, and `vcov()`, `summary()`, `confint()`,
`tidy()` and the delta-method standard errors of `margEffTable()` all use
it.

* `"normal"` (default): the inverse of the negative Hessian of the
  log-likelihood. It is valid when the model is correctly specified,
  including the count distribution.
* `"robust"`: the sandwich estimator. It remains valid for the mean
  coefficients when the distribution is misspecified but the mean model is
  right (quasi-likelihood). It does not rescue estimates from a wrong mean
  model (they are then estimates of something else, whatever their standard
  errors), and with sampling weights it is not a full survey-design analysis
  (strata, clusters and finite-population corrections are not modelled). For
  panel models (`countreg_rp()` with `group_var`, `renb()`, `poisLind.re()`,
  `repois()`, `negmultinom()`) the log-likelihood has one contribution per
  panel, so these standard errors are cluster-robust; for `countreg()` they
  are computed row by row and do not account for repeated observations of
  the same unit.
* `"boot"`: a nonparametric bootstrap with `bootstraps` replicates. Rows are
  resampled for `countreg()`, and whole panels for panel models. Use it
  when the sample is small, when the Hessian is close to singular, or as a
  check of the other two.

```{r stderr}
f <- Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + lnlength + speed50
nb_h <- countreg(f, d, family = "NB2", method = "BFGS")
nb_r <- countreg(f, d, family = "NB2", method = "BFGS", stderr = "robust")
set.seed(1)
nb_b <- countreg(f, d, family = "NB2", method = "BFGS", stderr = "boot",
                 bootstraps = 50)
round(cbind(Hessian = sqrt(diag(vcov(nb_h))),
            robust = sqrt(diag(vcov(nb_r))),
            bootstrap = sqrt(diag(vcov(nb_b)))), 4)
```

Similar standard errors, as here, are reassuring. A robust standard error
that is much larger than the Hessian one points to a misspecified
distribution or dependence between observations.

The bootstrap uses only replicates whose refit converged and gave finite
estimates. The number used is stored, with the reasons for any failures:

```{r boot-info}
nb_b$model$n_boot_ok
nb_b$model$boot_failures
```

If many replicates fail, increase `max.iters`, try another `method`, or
simplify the model. If fewer than two succeed, the standard errors are `NA`.

**Weights.** Every estimator takes `weights`, which are frequency weights
by default: a row with weight 3 counts as three independent observations. The
estimates, log-likelihood, robust covariance and BIC are those of the
expanded data. In panel models the weights belong to the panels (a panel
with weight 3 counts as three independent panels), so they must be constant
within a panel. The bootstrap resamples the expanded observations: it draws
new frequencies from a multinomial distribution and refits with them in
place of the weights, so it needs whole-number weights. Survey or
inverse-probability weights are declared with `weight_type = "sampling"`
(in `countreg()` and `countreg_rp()`): robust standard errors are then the
default and do not depend on the scale of the weights, and LR tests, AIC
and BIC are flagged as not valid.

## Marginal effects

`margEffTable()` reports average marginal effects (or elasticities) with
delta-method standard errors, or bootstrap standard errors with
`se = "bootstrap"`. For an indicator variable the default is the
pseudo-elasticity, the percentage change in the expected count.

```{r margeff}
margEffTable(nb_h, digits = 4)
```

The bootstrap of `margEffTable()` resamples the model's independent units
(rows, or panels for panel models, or the clusters in `cluster_var`) and
refits the model without an inner bootstrap.

## Prediction

`predict()` returns one value per row of `newdata`, in order. Rows with
missing values give `NA`; factor levels, contrasts and data-dependent bases
such as `poly()` and `splines::ns()` are those of the training data; offset
columns must be present.

For `countreg()` models, `type` chooses the quantity:

| `type` | Quantity |
|---|---|
| `"response"` (default) | expected observed count |
| `"true"` | expected true count (with underreporting) |
| `"prob_reported"` | probability that a count is reported |
| `"link"` | linear predictor \(X\beta\) + offset |
| `"prob"` | matrix of \(P(Y = k)\), \(k = 0, \dots,\) `max_count` |
| `"zero"` | zero-model probability (zero-inflated or hurdle models) |

```{r predict}
nd <- d[1:3, ]
predict(nb_h, newdata = nd)
round(predict(nb_h, newdata = nd, type = "prob", max_count = 4,
              overflow = TRUE), 3)
```

With `overflow = TRUE` the last column holds \(P(Y > \) `max_count`\()\), so
each row sums to one.

For random-parameter models, `method` chooses how the random coefficients
are handled:

* `"Simulated"` (default): the average over Halton draws.
* `"Exact"`: the closed-form expectation (Wood and Gayah, 2025). It is not
  available, and the prediction is infinite, when the expected value does
  not exist (a lognormal random parameter with a positive variable, or a
  gamma random parameter beyond its moment-generating function's domain);
  `"Simulated"` reports the same cases.
* `"Individual"` (or `"EB"`): Empirical Bayes predictions that condition on
  each panel's observed outcomes, so `newdata` must contain the outcome and
  the panel id. These are not forecasts for new units.

Negative multinomial models have `method = "Standard"` and `"EB"` in the
same sense.

## Three different intervals

Three intervals answer three different questions, and are easily confused:

| Interval | Question | How |
|---|---|---|
| Confidence interval for a coefficient | How uncertain is an estimated effect? | `confint()`, `tidy(conf.int = TRUE)` |
| Confidence interval for the expected count | How uncertain is the estimated mean at given covariates? | `predict(interval = "confidence")` |
| Prediction interval for a new count | Where is one new observation at given covariates likely to fall? | `predict(interval = "prediction")` |

```{r intervals}
confint(nb_h)["speed50", ]
nd2 <- data.frame(lnaadt = log(c(3000, 15000)), lnlength = 0, speed50 = 1)
predict(nb_h, newdata = nd2, interval = "confidence")
predict(nb_h, newdata = nd2, interval = "prediction", level = 0.9)
```

The confidence interval for the mean narrows as the sample grows; the
prediction interval does not, because a new count varies around its mean
whatever the sample size. Prediction-interval limits are whole counts and,
because counts are discrete, usually cover a little more than the stated
level. Both intervals for `countreg()` models account for estimation
uncertainty using the asymptotic normal distribution of the estimates,
evaluated at deterministic Halton points (or a parametric bootstrap with
`uncertainty = "bootstrap"`); see `?predict.flexCountReg`.

A fourth kind, a *tolerance interval*, is meant to contain at least a stated
share of all counts at given covariates (for example 90% of road segments
with these characteristics) with a stated confidence; see
`?tolerance_interval`.

## Fitted values, residuals and simulation

`fitted()` gives the predictions for the rows used in estimation, and
`residuals()` the residuals of three types:

* `"response"`: observed minus fitted.
* `"pearson"`: divided by the standard deviation implied by the fitted
  distribution (`countreg()` models).
* `"quantile"`: randomized quantile residuals (Dunn and Smyth, 1996), which
  are standard normal when the model is correct; use them for residual
  plots and normality checks.

```{r residuals}
r <- residuals(nb_h, type = "quantile")
c(mean = mean(r), sd = sd(r))
```

`simulate()` draws new responses from the fitted distribution for the same
rows (with `seed`, reproducible and without changing the random-number
stream of the session). The parameters are held at their estimates (a
plug-in simulation), so the spread of simulated statistics reflects the
randomness of the counts, not the uncertainty of the estimates. It is the
basis of parametric-bootstrap checks:

```{r simulate}
sims <- simulate(nb_h, nsim = 200, seed = 1)
# Observed share of zeros against its simulated distribution
c(observed = mean(d$Total_crashes == 0),
  simulated = mean(colMeans(sims == 0)))
```

`tidy()`, `glance()` and `augment()` return tidy data frames, and
`rootogram()` and `cureplot()` compare the fitted distribution and mean
with the data (see the vignette on choosing a count distribution).

## Comparing models

### AIC and BIC

AIC and BIC compare any models fit to the same observations, nested or not,
and are always reported. BIC uses the number of independent units: rows,
panels for panel models, and the sum of the frequency weights when weights
are used.

```{r glance}
po <- countreg(f, d, family = "POISSON", method = "BFGS")
nb1 <- countreg(f, d, family = "NB1", method = "BFGS")
pl <- countreg(f, d, family = "PL", method = "BFGS")
do.call(rbind, lapply(list(Poisson = po, NB1 = nb1, NB2 = nb_h, PL = pl),
                      function(m) glance(m)[, c("logLik", "AIC", "BIC")]))
```

### Likelihood-ratio tests

An LR test compares a restricted model with a larger one. The statistic
\(2(\ell_\text{full} - \ell_\text{restricted})\) has its usual chi-square
distribution only when:

1. **The models are nested.** The restricted model is the larger model with
   some parameters fixed: the same estimator and model components, the
   restricted model's parameters a subset of the larger model's, and the
   same family or a nested family.
2. **The restriction is regular.** The fixed values are inside the parameter
   space, every remaining parameter is identified under the restriction,
   and the restriction is not reached only in a limit.
3. **The data are the same.** The same observations, outcome, offsets,
   weights and panels, and the same values of the variables both models use.
4. **Both fits reached their maximum.** Both report convergence, and the
   larger model's log-likelihood is not below the restricted model's.

The families nest as follows:

| Restricted | Larger | Restriction | Null distribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| Poisson | NB1, NB2, PLN, PIG1, PIG2, PIG | dispersion = 0 | 50:50 mixture of \(\chi^2_{df-1}\) and \(\chi^2_{df}\) |
| Poisson | GP1, GP2 | dispersion = 0 | \(\chi^2_{df}\) |
| Poisson | COM | \(\nu = 1\) | \(\chi^2_{df}\) |
| Poisson | DPO, HYPERPOIS, GAMMACOUNT | \(\phi = 1\), \(\gamma = 1\), shape \(= 1\) | \(\chi^2_{df}\) |
| NB1, NB2 | NBP | \(P = 1\) or \(P = 2\) | \(\chi^2_{df}\) |
| PL | PLG, PLL | \(\alpha = 0\), \(\sigma = 0\) | 50:50 mixture |

For NB1, NB2 and the other families in the first row, a dispersion of 0 is
on the boundary of the parameter space (a dispersion cannot be negative).
The statistic then has a 50:50 mixture distribution, and the ordinary
chi-square p-value would be twice too large.

These comparisons are **not** valid, and no p-value is reported:

* **Poisson vs PL, PLG or PLL.** The Poisson-Lindley family does not contain
  the Poisson distribution: its variance is at least
  \(\mu + \mu^2/2\) for every \(\theta\).
* **Poisson vs NBP or SI.** At the Poisson limit, NBP's power \(P\) and the
  Sichel \(\gamma\) are not identified, so the usual asymptotics fail.
* **Poisson vs PW, PGE or GW.** Their distributions approach Poisson only as
  a parameter goes to infinity.
* **Poisson vs DELAPORTE, HERMITE, PA or NBGE.** Poisson is reached only at
  the edge of the parameter space (a share of 0 on the logit scale, or a
  dispersion going to zero), where other parameters are not identified.
* **A boundary family with a dispersion formula.** The restriction sends an
  intercept to minus infinity while the slopes become unidentified.
* **Models with and without a zero model or underreporting.** No zero
  inflation, or full reporting, is reached only in a limit (an intercept of
  minus or plus infinity on the logit scale).
* **Models with different random parameters.** A random-parameter variance
  of zero is on the boundary, often with other parameters unidentified.
* **Non-nested models**, such as NB1 vs NB2.

For these, compare models with AIC and BIC, or with a parametric bootstrap
of the LR statistic using `simulate()`.

`summary()` reports a test against Poisson when it is valid:

```{r summary-lr}
summary(nb_h)$lr_test
is.null(summary(pl)$lr_test)   # no test: PL does not nest Poisson
```

When a condition fails, `regCompTest()` reports no LR test and gives the
reason in `LR_reason`. Nesting of the mean model is checked on the design
matrices, so `y ~ x` is nested in `y ~ I(2 * x) + z`.

`regCompTest()` applies the same rules to two fitted models (the one with
fewer parameters is the restricted model) or to a model and a base model it
fits on the same rows:

```{r regcomptest}
r <- regCompTest(po, model2 = nb_h)
r[c("LR", "LRdof", "LR_type", "LR_pvalue")]
r <- regCompTest(nb1, model2 = countreg(f, d, family = "NBP",
                                        method = "BFGS"))
r[c("LR", "LRdof", "LR_type", "LR_pvalue")]
```

When the larger model has the lower log-likelihood, the larger model did
not reach its maximum (check its convergence), and no p-value is given.

### McFadden's pseudo-R²

`regCompTest()` and `regCompTable()` report McFadden's pseudo-R²,
\(1 - \ell / \ell_0\), against an intercept-only Poisson model on the same
rows by default, so it is comparable across families. `basemodel` and
`variables` choose another baseline.

```{r table}
regCompTable(list(Poisson = po, NB2 = nb_h))
```

## Next steps

* `vignette("getting-started", package = "flexCountReg")` applies these
  tools in a complete analysis.
* `vignette("diagnosing-count-models", package = "flexCountReg")` covers
  residuals, rootograms and held-out comparisons.
* `vignette("random-parameters-and-panels", package = "flexCountReg")`
  explains the independent unit for repeated observations: the
  `washington_roads` rows used here are segment-years, so the row-level
  standard errors above treat repeated years of a segment as independent.
* `vignette("predictions-and-effects", package = "flexCountReg")`
  interprets predictions and marginal effects in detail.
* `vignette("prediction-for-panel-data", package = "flexCountReg")`
  separates predictions for new and for known units in panels.
